pages.title: ECG History
pages.text:
ECG History
▪Electrocardiograph vs electrocardiogram
▪Instrument used to record electrical activity of the heart
▪The graphic representation of the heart’s electrical activity
▪Precursors to the ECG
▪1786 – Dr Luigi Galvani first noted electrical current in 
skeletal muscle
▪1842 – Dr. Carlo Matteucci demonstrated electrical current 
accompanying the heartbeat in frogs
▪1877 – Augustus Waller
▪Published first human ECG using a capillary electrometer
▪Electrodes were placed on the chest and back

pages.title: ECG History 1842 – Dr. Carlo Matteucci
pages.text:
ECG History 1842 – Dr. Carlo Matteucci 
▪The heart produces measurable electrical currents
▪He connected the beating heart of a frog to a sensitive galvanometer (a device that detects electric 
current).
▪Deflections on the instrument synchronized with each heartbeat.
▪ Electrical activity continues even after removal from the body
▪A frog heart removed from the animal still produced electrical signals as long as it continued to beat.
▪This proved that the heart’s electricity is intrinsic, not dependent on the nervous system.

pages.title: ECG History 1842 – Dr. Carlo Matteucci
pages.text:
ECG History 1842 – Dr. Carlo Matteucci
▪The heart’s electrical discharge can stimulate another muscle
▪In one famous demonstration, Matteucci connected a beating heart to the 
leg of another frog. 
▪Each heartbeat caused the leg to twitch — a dramatic visual proof that the 
heart generates electrical impulses strong enough to activate other tissues.
▪Work lead to eventual development of the EKG

pages.title: ECG History 1842 – Dr. Carlo Matteucci
pages.text:
ECG History 1842 – Dr. Carlo Matteucci
▪Matteucci’s findings were revolutionary because they showed:
▪The heart is not just a mechanical pump; it is an electrical organ.
▪Heartbeats are triggered by electrical impulses, not by direct nerve 
commands.
▪These impulses can be measured, which later inspired:
▪Augustus Waller’s early electrocardiograms (1880s)
▪Willem Einthoven’s string galvanometer (1902)

pages.title: ECG History 1877 – Augustus Waller
pages.text:
ECG History 1877 – Augustus Waller
▪Recorded the first human ECG (1887)
▪Waller attached electrodes to a human subject 
(famously including his dog “Jimmy” in 
demonstrations) and connected them to a capillary 
electrometer.
▪This device converted tiny voltage changes into 
movements of a mercury column, producing a crude 
ECG trace.
▪Used five lead locations
▪Upper and lower extremities
▪Mouth

pages.title: ECG History 1877 – Augustus Waller
pages.text:
ECG History 1877 – Augustus Waller
▪Demonstrated that the heart’s electrical activity can be measured externally
▪Waller showed that the heart’s electrical signals could be detected without surgery, 
simply by placing electrodes on the skin.
▪Proof that surface electrocardiography was feasible.

pages.title: ECG History 1877 – Augustus Waller
pages.text:
ECG History 1877 – Augustus Waller
▪Waller himself was skeptical about the clinical value of ECGs, but history proved 
otherwise.
▪Inspired Willem Einthoven, who later invented the string galvanometer and produced the 
first clinically useful ECGs (earning the 1924 Nobel Prize)

pages.title: ECG History 1902 - Willem Einthoven
pages.text:
ECG History 1902 - Willem Einthoven
▪Credited for inventing the electrocardiograph in 1902
▪The string galvanometer
▪Fine, silver 
coated quartz filament suspended in a magnetic field
▪Heart's electrical impulses passed through the filament
▪Movement was magnified and recorded on photographic
paper
▪Won Nobel Peace prize in 1924

TOPOGRAPHIC ANATOMY
▪Topographic anatomy, also known as regional anatomy
▪Focuses on the study of the relationships between different structures 
within specific regions of the body. 
▪Understanding the topography of anatomical structures is 
essential for:
▪Identifying anatomical landmarks for surgical procedures
▪Understanding the pathways of blood vessels and nerves
▪Localizing injuries or diseases within a specific body region
▪Guiding the administration of injections or other interventions
▪BOTTOMLINE:  WHERE LEADS NEED TO BE PLACED!

▪Provides a common language to

pages.title: TOPOGRAPHIC ANATOMY
pages.text:
TOPOGRAPHIC ANATOMY
▪Before x-ray was invented in 1895, we 
only had inspection, auscultation, 
palpation and percussion to assess 
underlying structures
▪Directional terms describe the positions 
of structures relative to other structures 
or locations in the body
▪Superficial landmarks serve as guides to 
structures that lie beneath

pages.title: TOPOGRAPHIC ANATOMY
pages.text:
TOPOGRAPHIC ANATOMY
▪Commonly used directional terms include:
▪Superior (Cranial): Toward the head or upper part of the body.
▪Inferior (Caudal): Away from the head or toward the lower part of the 
body.
▪Anterior (Ventral): Toward the front of the body.
▪Posterior (Dorsal): Toward the back of the body.
▪Medial: Toward the midline of the body.
▪Lateral: Away from the midline of the body.
▪Proximal: Closer to the point of attachment or to the trunk of the body.
▪Distal: Farther from the point of attachment or from the trunk of the 
body.
▪Superficial: Toward or on the surface of the body.
▪Deep: Away from the surface, further into the body.

pages.title: Systems of the Body
pages.text:
Systems of the Body
• The human body is built in this format:
• Cells make up tissues
• Tissues make up organs
• Organs make up organ systems
• Organ systems make up an organism
• Homeostasis is when the body maintains a 
stable and balanced environment.
• Critical for this is ph level of body

pages.title: Maintaining Homeostasis
pages.text:
Maintaining Homeostasis
▪pH is a measure of how acidic or basic a substance is 
▪It reflects the balance between acids and bases in the body
▪Normal blood pH is slightly alkaline
▪Normal range: 7.35 – 7.45
▪Even small changes outside this range can disrupt normal body 
function
• Abnormal pH can affect: 
• Oxygen delivery
• Heart function
• Brain function
• Overall cellular metabolism
▪The body uses the respiratory system (CO₂ removal) and 
cardiovascular system to help keep pH within a safe range

pages.title: The Respiratory System
pages.text:
The Respiratory System
• The respiratory system provides the 
“hardware” that is required to bring Oxygen 
(O2) into the body and remove Carbon Dioxide 
(CO2) from the body to assist the body in 
meeting it’s HOMEOSTATIC needs.
• Carbon Dioxide is important to the body but it’s 
a waste product for the respiratory system.
• The ONLY way to oxygenate the blood is 
through RESPIRATION.

pages.title: The Respiratory System
pages.text:
The Respiratory System
▪CO₂ plays a key role in 
regulating blood pH
▪Increased CO₂ → increased 
acidity (↓ pH)
▪Decreased CO₂ → decreased 
acidity (↑ pH)
▪The respiratory system helps 
maintain acid–base balance by 
controlling how much CO₂ is 
removed from the body

pages.title: The Respiratory System
pages.text:
The Respiratory System
• Essential for human life
• Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide between the body and 
the environment
• Understanding its anatomy and physiology is crucial for 
appreciating how the body obtains the oxygen necessary 
for cellular function and removes the waste product, 
carbon dioxide
• Works in conjunction with the Cardiovascular system
• Provides oxygen to the blood to deliver to the cells of the 
body 
• Removes the carbon dioxide waste from the blood to expel 
to the environment

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
• The main function of the upper airways is conditioning, and 
cleaning of the air conducted to the lower airways. 
• The upper airway also plays an important role in the protection 
of the lower airways and formation of the sound produced by the 
vocal cords.
• Shares structures with the Digestive System

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
▪NASOPHARYNX
▪Nose and Nasal Cavity
▪The primary entryway for air, where it is filtered, 
warmed, and humidified.
▪OROPHARYNX
▪Mouth and Oral Cavity
▪Not optimal for ventilation
▪Can breathe larger volumes but does not filter or 
humidify.

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
▪HYPOPHARYNX
▪A muscular tube (throat) that serves as a 
passageway for both air (to the larynx) and food (to 
the esophagus)
▪Epiglottis responsible for this process

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – The Epiglottis
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – The Epiglottis
▪Protects lower airway and directs 
food and liquid to digestive 
system

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Upper Airway
▪LARYNX
▪May be known as the voice box
▪Routes air into the lower respiratory tract and houses 
the vocal cords

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
▪The lower airway’s main function is gas exchange
▪Trachea: Commonly called the windpipe, the trachea is 
a rigid tube that directs air into the lungs.
▪Bronchi and Bronchioles: The trachea splits into the 
right and left bronchi, which branch into smaller 
bronchioles within the lungs, distributing air to all 
regions.
▪Lungs: Two spongy organs (right and left lungs)
▪Right has three lobes
▪Left has two lobes
▪Alveoli: Tiny air sacs at the ends of bronchioles. These 
are the primary sites for the exchange of gases.

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
▪Deadspace
▪No gas exchange takes place in the other structures of the 
respiratory system
▪Air moves through the structures but there is NO gas exchange
▪Even though air contains oxygen and carbon dioxide, gas 
exchange requires alveoli and surrounding blood vessels.
▪Purpose of the dead space is to move air and into 
the alveoli.
▪Increased dead space means less effective oxygen 
delivery, even if breathing appears normal

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
▪Gas exchange takes place in the 
terminal bronchioles and alveoli 
where blood vessels intertwine
▪Ventilation (2 Phases)
▪Inspiration
▪Exhalation
▪Movement of air through the 
deadspace to the alveoli
▪Conditions that impair alveoli—such 
as fluid, collapse, or inflammation—
can severely reduce oxygenation 
despite visible chest rise

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
pages.text: Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
▪Pleura
▪Two Layers
▪Parietal layer
▪Visceral layer
▪Pleural Fluid
▪Purpose:
▪The pleural cavity serves to facilitate lung movement
▪Provide a lubricated space that reduces friction
▪Allow for optimal expansion and contraction of the lungs
▪Fluid accumulation, air in the pleural space, or 
inflammation can interfere with lung expansion, 
leading to breathing difficulty even if the airways 
themselves are clear

pages.title: Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
pages.text:
Respiratory Anatomy – Lower Airway
▪Diaphragm
▪Dome shaped muscle
▪Primary muscle of breathing
▪Separates the abdominal and thoracic cavities
▪Expands downward during inspiration allowing lungs to 
expand
▪During relaxation returns to original position
▪Injury, paralysis, or fatigue of the diaphragm can 
severely impair ventilation, even if the lungs and airways 
themselves are normal

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
▪Diaphragm and intercostal muscles are the primary muscles of breathing. 
▪Also involved are:
▪Neck (cervical muscles)
▪Abdominal muscles
▪Pectoral muscles

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
▪Ventilation is driven by changes 
in thoracic volume that create 
pressure gradients between the 
lungs and the atmosphere
▪At higher altitudes, ventilation 
still occurs due to pressure 
differences, but reduced 
atmospheric pressure lowers 
oxygen availability, requiring 
increased respiratory effort.

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
▪Ventilation and respiration are two separate, interdependent functions of 
the respiratory system. 
▪Ventilation is simple air movement into (INHALATION) and out (EXHALATION) 
of the lungs.
▪Requires chest rise and fall
▪May be done naturally or mechanically
▪Inhalation (Inspiration): The diaphragm contracts and moves 
downward, while the intercostal muscles expand the rib cage. This 
increases thoracic cavity volume and decreases pressure, drawing 
air into the lungs.
▪Exhalation (Expiration): The diaphragm and intercostal muscles 
relax, decreasing thoracic volume and increasing pressure, 
pushing air out of the lungs.

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
VENTILATION

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
▪Respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the terminal 
bronchioles/alveoli and tissues (cellular respiration)
▪The alveoli is where the cardiovascular system and respiratory system work 
together
 
▪Dead space: the portion of the respiratory system that has no alveoli and 
where little or no exchange of gas between air and blood occurs
▪There is only movement of air in or out even though oxygen and carbon 
dioxide are present.

pages.text:

RESPIRATION

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
Diffusion is the passive movement of 
molecules from an area of higher 
concentration to an area of lower 
concentration, driven by the concentration 
gradient. 
Diseases or conditions that damage alveoli, 
thicken membranes, or fill air sacs with fluid 
can slow or block diffusion, leading to poor 
oxygenation even when breathing appears 
adequate

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
▪Diffusion
▪High concentration to Low 
concentration
▪PASSIVE Transportation (Movement)
▪Requires NO energy
▪Occurs in the alveoli in the 
respiratory system
▪Can be inhibited by Lung 
diseases, injury and other factors
▪Increases stress on cardiovascular 
system and potentially other body 
systems

pages.title: Respiratory Physiology
pages.text:
Respiratory Physiology
▪The brain stem controls breathing
▪Medulla Oblongata and Pons
▪Ventilation cycles (RATE) are initiated by chemoreceptors (monitor 
increase in CO2) in the ventral medulla based on carbon dioxide 
levels and pH levels in the cerebral spinal fluid
▪Other areas of the brain stem help augment the rate during 
emotional or physical stress
▪Vagus nerve increases respiratory rate, tidal volume and minute ventilation 
(amount of air that enters the lungs in a minute)
▪Other receptors in the body serve as “back ups” by monitoring O2, 
CO2 and pH

pages.title: Monitoring Respiratory Status

Monitoring Respiratory Status
▪Respiratory Rate
▪Normal respiratory rate for adults 
is 12 – 20 breaths per minute
▪Some places say 12 – 16
▪Infants and childrens rates are 
faster
▪Displayed using readings from the 
ECG Leads

pages.title: Monitoring Respiratory Status
pages.text:
Monitoring Respiratory Status
▪Pulse oximetry  (SpO2)
▪Noninvasive and provides estimate 
of Oxygen Saturation in the blood
▪Oxygen is classified as a drug and 
should be dosed as such
▪“SpO₂ tells us how full the buses 
are—not how many buses we 
have.”

pages.title: Monitoring Respiratory Status
pages.text:
Monitoring Respiratory Status
▪Pulse oximetry limitations
▪Abnormalities i.e., sickle cell 
anemia
▪Barriers i.e., fingernail polish, 
pigmentation of skin, sepsis
▪Poisoning i.e., carbon monoxide
▪Displayed as waveform and/or 
numeric value, may display HR
▪Normal range 94 – 99%

pages.title: Monitoring Respiratory Status
pages.text:
Monitoring Respiratory Status
Pulse Oximetry
• A Pulse oximeter is clipped to the tip of your 
finger 
• It uses a Sensor that consists of two light 
sources red (absorbed by deoxygenated 
blood) 
• infrared (absorbed by oxygenated blood) and 
a photodetector to measure the absorption 
of visible light.
• Oxygenated and De-oxygenated hemoglobin 
have different light absorption rates.
• The sensors of the pulse oximeter detect the 
level of blood oxygen saturation or SpO2. 
depending on the light passed through it. 
• The device then displays the percentage of 
oxygen on the screen of the pulse oximeter.
Key Point Review:  Normal 02 saturation range 
94% - 99%

pages.title: Monitoring Respiratory Status
pages.text:
Monitoring Respiratory Status
Pulse Oximetry
• Onset of oxygen toxicity varies
• Based on the type of exposure
• Central nervous system (CNS) toxicity
• potentially occurring within minutes under
high pressure
• Pulmonary toxicity may develop over several 
hours to days
Key Point Review:  Normal 02 saturation range

• The heart is enclosed in a double-walled sac called the 
pericardium (peri = around, cardi = heart)
• The loosely fitting superficial part of this sac is the 
fibrous pericardium
• This tough, dense connective tissue layer:
• Protects the heart

layers is the slit like pericardial 
cavity, which contains about a 
tablespoon of serous fluid.

• The serous membranes, lubricated 
by the fluid, glide smoothly past one 
another, allowing the mobile heart 
to work in a relatively friction-free 
environment

contains the blood vessels and nerves

containing muscle cells for contraction

a single layer of cells containing nerves 
and coronary blood vessels as well as 
electrical component

pages.text:
• The “discharging” chambers
• Their walls are much more massive than 
the atrial walls, reflecting the difference in 
function between the atria and ventricles
• When the ventricles contract, they propel 
blood out of the heart into the circulation
• The right ventricle pumps blood into the 
pulmonary artery, which routes the blood to the 
lungs where gas exchange occurs

pages.text:
Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
Stroke Volume (SV)
• Stroke volume is the amount of blood ejected by the left ventricle 
during each heartbeat. 
• Factors influencing stroke volume include preload (amount), 
afterload (resist), and contractility (strength) of the heart muscle. 
• A healthy stroke volume typically ranges between 60 to 100 
milliliters per beat. 
• Variations in stroke volume often indicate cardiac dysfunction.

pages.title: Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
pages.text:
Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
Heart Rate (HR)
• Heart rate represents the number of heartbeats per minute. 
• It is a simple yet essential parameter for cardiac assessment, 
with normal resting heart rates ranging from 60 to 100 beats per 
minute (bpm) for adults. 
• Abnormal heart rates, such as bradycardia (slow heart rate) or 
tachycardia (fast heart rate), may signal underlying heart 
conditions.

pages.title: Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
pages.text:
Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
Cardiac Output (CO)
• Cardiac output refers to the amount of blood the heart pumps in one minute. 
• CO = Stroke Volume (SV) x Heart Rate (HR)
• Measured in liters per minute (L/min), normal cardiac output ranges between 4 to 8 L/min 
for an average adult. This parameter is crucial for understanding the heart's ability to meet 
the body's oxygen and nutrient demands.

pages.title: Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
pages.text:
Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
Ejection Fraction (EF)
• EF is a measurement to indicate how well the heart pumps blood
• Percentage ejected from the ventricles with each heartbeat
• Normal is 55 – 70%
• Low EF may indicate heart problems to include heart failure
• Measured typically using echocardiogram, cardiac MRI or nuclear stress test
• In some cases, a normal EF may still be present in heart failure due to stiffening of heart 
muscle

pages.text:

• Blood flows through the heart in one direction: from 
atria to ventricles and out the great arteries leaving 
the superior aspect of the heart
• Four valves enforce this one-way traffic
• They open and close in response to differences in 
blood pressure on their two sides
• The four valves are:
• Atrioventricular (AV) Valves
•
Tricuspid Valve
•
Mitral valve (Bicuspid)
• Semilunar (SL) Valves
•
Pulmonic Valve

Atrioventricular (AV) Valves
• The two atrioventricular (AV) valves, one 
located at each atrial-ventricular junction,

the mitral valve. This valve is also known as 
the bicuspid valve

white collagen cords called chordae 
tendinae or “heart strings”, which anchor 
the cusps to the papillary muscles 
protruding from the ventricular walls

together
• Atresia. In this condition, the valve isn't formed, 
and a solid sheet of tissue blocks the blood flow 
between the heart chambers

respiration take place

“merge,” and “converge” into the successively larger vessels 
approaching the heart

Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
 The Heart: The Pump 
•The heart’s job is to generate pressure.
•Each beat pushes blood forward, creating the force needed to move it through the vessels.
•Think of it as the engine that keeps the whole system moving.
 Blood Volume: The Fuel (Fluid)
•Blood volume is the amount of blood circulating in your body.
•Enough volume is essential for the heart to create proper pressure.
•Too little volume → pressure drops, organs don’t get enough blood.
•Too much volume → the heart works harder, and vessels can become strained.
 Blood Vessels: The Pathways (Pipes)
•Arteries, veins, and capillaries act as the network of tubes that carry blood everywhere.
•Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure.
•Veins bring blood back to the heart under lower pressure.
•Capillaries allow exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste with tissues. (Cellular Respiration)

pages.title: Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
pages.text:
Cardiovascular System Anatomy and Physiology
1. The heart pumps blood into the vessels.
•
Pressure from the heart pushes blood through arteries.
2. Blood volume determines how much pressure the heart can generate.
•
If volume drops (like dehydration or bleeding), pressure falls and the heart must beat faster.
3. Blood vessels adjust their diameter to control flow and pressure.
•
They can constrict (narrow) to raise blood pressure.
•
They can dilate (widen) to lower blood pressure.
4. Together, they maintain circulation.
•
Oxygen delivery
•
Waste removal
•
Temperature regulation
•
Nutrient transport

pages.title: Cardiac Electrical System
pages.text:
Cardiac Electrical System
▪In a normal, healthy heart impulses are initiated in 
the sinoatrial (SA) node
▪SA node is the natural pacemaker of the heart
▪Grouping of cells known as pacemaker cells and located 
in the wall of the right atrium
▪SA node inherit rate is 60 – 100
▪Impulse is sent across the atria causing them to 
contract
▪Intraatrial pathways – spread across the atria
▪Internodal pathway – Impulse is sent from SA node to 
the next component of the system

pages.title: Cardiac Electrical System
pages.text:
Cardiac Electrical System
▪The Atrioventricular (AV) Node/Junction and Bundle of His
▪Located near the center of the heart where both atria and ventricles 
are near each other
▪Controls the transmission of the impulse sent from the SA node
▪Coordinates the contraction of the atria and ventricles
▪Delays impulse to allow atria to completely contract and expel 
blood to the ventricles
▪Serves as a “back-up” pacemaker in the event of SA node failure 
with a rate of 40 - 60
▪Impulse is “delayed” long enough through the AV node, Bundle of 
His and through the Bundle Branches to their terminating points 
allowing ventricles to completely fill and be ready to contract.

pages.title: Cardiac Electrical System
pages.text:
Cardiac Electrical System
▪The final point of the conduction system is the Purkinje 
(PUR-KIN-GEE) fibers
▪Located in the ventricular walls and are electrically 
excitable cells
▪Responsible for impulse that causes the ventricles to 
contract and discharge blood
▪In the event both SA and AV nodes fail, the ventricles 
will attempt to control the heart
▪Rate is only 20 – 40

▪Cycle Breakdown:

▪Atrioventricular Delay: The AV node temporarily slows conduction to

▪Repolarization: Both atria and ventricles return to a resting state, 
preparing for the next cycle.

pages.title: Cardiac Electrical System
pages.text:
Cardiac Electrical System
▪Medications that affect cardiac electrical conduction are often used 
to manage arrhythmias and other heart conditions
▪Antiarrhythmic Drugs: These medications are used to treat abnormal 
heart rhythms. They work by altering the electrical impulses in the heart. 
Examples include amiodarone, lidocaine, and procainamide
▪Beta-Blockers: These drugs reduce the heart rate and the force of 
contraction by blocking the effects of adrenaline. Common beta-blockers 
include metoprolol, atenolol, and propranolol
▪Calcium Channel Blockers: These medications prevent calcium from 
entering the cells of the heart and blood vessel walls, leading to lower 
heart rate and blood pressure. Examples include verapamil and diltiazem

pages.title: Cardiac Electrical System
pages.text:
Cardiac Electrical System
Digitalis Glycosides: These drugs increase the force of the heart's 
contractions.  Digoxin is a well-known example
Sodium Channel Blockers: These medications slow the electrical 
conduction in the heart by blocking sodium channels. Examples 
include quinidine and flecainide
Medications are prescribed based on the specific needs and 
conditions of the patient, and their use should be closely monitored 
by a healthcare professional.

Nervous System Influence
▪The sympathetic nervous system is responsible for fight-or-flight 
response
▪Sends commands to adrenal glands
▪Epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine (noradrenaline) are 
secreted to stimulate heart and blood vessels.
▪HR speeds up, respiration increase, vasodilation
▪The parasympathetic nervous system also has effects on the 
cardiovascular system.
▪Addresses actions that do not require an immediate response
▪HR slows down, respirations decrease, vasoconstriction
▪Vagus nerve

REST and DIGEST

pages.title: Hormonal Influence
pages.text:
Hormonal Influence
▪Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH): Also known as vasopressin, ADH is 
released by the pituitary gland. It promotes water retention by the 
kidneys, which increases blood volume and, consequently, blood 
pressure. ADH also causes vasoconstriction
▪Aldosterone: This hormone is produced by the adrenal cortex and 
helps regulate blood pressure by increasing sodium and water 
reabsorption in the kidneys. This increases blood volume and 
pressure
▪Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP): Released by the atria of the 
heart, ANP reduces blood volume and pressure by promoting 
sodium and water excretion by the kidneys. It also causes 
vasodilation

pages.title: Cardiac Vectors and Leads

Cardiac Vectors and Leads
▪A cardiac vector represents the direction and magnitude of the 
heart’s electrical activity during depolarization and repolarization. 
It’s a key concept in understanding electrocardiograms (ECGs or 
EKGs) and interpreting the heart’s electrical axis.
▪Why It Matters: The heart’s electrical impulses don’t move 
randomly—they follow a specific path through the conduction 
system. Vectors help visualize this movement and are essential for 
interpreting ECGs.
▪Not everyone’s ECG looks identical
▪Identify the cardiac cycle and interpret based on findings

pages.title: Action Potentials
pages.text:
Action Potentials
•
Ions are small charged molecules that can move across the cell membrane 
through special ion channels
•
Cations are positively charged ions. Examples of cations are:
•
Sodium (Na+) (Normally extracellular)
•
Calcium (Ca2+) (Normally extracellular)
•
Potassium (K+) (Normally intracellular)
•
Magnesium (Mg2+) (Normally intracellular)
•
Anions are negatively charged ions. Examples of anions are:
•
Chloride
•
Bicarbonate
•
Phosphate

pages.title: Action Potentials
pages.text:
Action Potentials
• Because ions are charged molecules, an electrical gradient is also established across 
the cell membrane, transforming each cell into a tiny battery
• This imbalance in electrical charge across the cell membrane is known as the resting 
membrane potential
• Every cell in our body is slightly more negative on the inside than the outside
• The resting membrane potential of most cells range between -70 and -90 mV 
(millivolts)

pages.title: Action Potentials
pages.text:
Action Potentials
• An action potential is a short-lasting event in which the electrical membrane 
potential of a cell rapidly rises and falls, causing several biochemical 
changes
• The action potential is brought on by a rapid change in membrane 
permeability to certain ions
• Excitable cells include neurons (nerve cells) and muscle cells

pages.title: The Sodium Pump
pages.text:
The Sodium Pump
•Restores Ion Balance After Action Potentials
•During each heartbeat, sodium enters cardiac cells during depolarization.
•The pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, using ATP to reset the ion gradient.
•This is essential for maintaining the resting membrane potential and allowing future action 
potentials.
•Supports Calcium Removal (Indirectly)
•The pump helps power the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, which removes calcium from the cell.
•This prevents excessive intracellular calcium accumulation and ensures proper relaxation after 
contraction.
•Regulates Cardiac Contractility
•When the pump’s activity is reduced (like in heart failure), intracellular Na⁺ rises, disrupting 
calcium handling.
•This can increase cardiac contractility (positive inotropic effect), but excessive dysfunction leads to 
arrhythmias.
•Target for Cardiac Drugs
•Digoxin, a common heart medication, inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.
•This leads to increased intracellular calcium, strengthening contractions—useful in heart failure.

Systematic Approach to Rhythm Interpretation
STEP FIVE
▪QRS measurement and analysis
▪Normal conduction through the 
pathways produces narrow complex
▪Measure from beginning of complex to 
J point
▪J point is point of transition into ST 
segment
▪Should be < 0.12 seconds
▪If slightly wider it is labeled as such
▪All should appear similar and constant 
measurement
▪Complex may NOT always have every 
wave but it is ALWAYS called the QRS 
complex
Start of complex to J point is 3 small boxes. 
0.04 x 3 = 0.12 seconds

Systematic Approach to Rhythm Interpretation
STEP SIX
▪QT interval measurement (QTi)
▪BEGINNING of QRS complex to 
the END of the T wave
▪Should be less than half the R – R 
measurement
▪Corrected for HR (QTc)
▪Bradycardia = longer
▪Tachycardia =  shorter
▪A long QT can delay repolarization 
and possibly put patient in danger 
of life-threatening rhythm
R to R is 19 small blocks, 19 x 0.04 = 0.76 seconds
QT interval is 10 small blocks, 10 x 0.04 = 0.40 seconds
QT corrected would be 0.43 seconds

pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Sinus Rhtyhm
• Atrial contraction is effective:
– The atria contract in a coordinated fashion.
– The “atrial kick”—which contributes ~20–30% of 
ventricular filling—is preserved.
• Ventricular filling is normal:
– Impulses reach the AV node and ventricles in a timely 
manner, ventricular contraction and cardiac output 
is normal.

pages.title: Clinical Implication
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Implication
Blood flow remains adequate and coordinated, and unless it's associated with 
underlying pathology (e.g., sinus node dysfunction or digoxin toxicity), it rarely 
requires treatment.
• Adequate Perfusion and Hemodynamic Stability
• Lower Risk of Thromboembolic Events
• Baseline for Identifying Abnormalities
• Not Always “Normal”

Blood Flow in Sinus Bradycardia
• A. Increased filling time
– Slower rate → longer diastole.
– Ventricles fill more completely.
– Stroke volume may increase slightly to compensate.
• B. Decreased cardiac output

pages.title: Clinical Implication of Sinus
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Implication of Sinus 
Bradycardia
• If the heart rate drops too low (often <50 bpm 
depending on the person), the body may not 
receive enough oxygenated blood. This is 
especially true in:
– Older adults
– Patients with heart failure
– Those on beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers
– Individuals with SA node dysfunction
• When stroke volume is high enough to maintain 
normal perfusion, it is not harmful

Mechanism of Sinus Tachycardia
The sinus node is the pacemaker, firing regularly at 
a rate of greater than 100 bpm. Each impulse is 
conducted normally through to the ventricles.

Rules for Sinus Tachycardia
• Regularity: Regular
• Rate: Greater than 100 bpm (usually does not 
exceed 160 bpm)
• P Wave: Uniform shape; one P wave in front of 
every QRS complex – present, upright, uniform
• PRI: 0.12–0.20 second and constant
• QRS: Less than 0.12 second

pages.title: Blood Flow in Sinus Tachycardia
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Sinus Tachycardia
• Shortened filling time
– Diastole (filling phase) becomes shorter.
– Ventricles have less time to fill.
– Stroke volume may decrease slightly because the chambers don’t 
fully fill.
• Increased cardiac output (up to a point)
• Potential drop in output if rate becomes too high
• Coronary perfusion occurs mostly during diastole.
– Diastole shortens → less time for coronary filling.
– This can stress the heart

pages.title: Clinical Implication of Sinus
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Implication of Sinus 
Tachycardia
• It’s often a normal physiological response:
– Exercise
– Stress
– Fever
– Pregnancy
– Pain
• In these cases, increased heart rate helps maintain or 
boost blood flow to tissues.

pages.title: Clinical Implication of Sinus
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Implication of Sinus 
Tachycardia
• When sinus tachycardia is a warning sign
– It may indicate:
▪Hypovolemia
▪Sepsis
▪Heart failure
▪Pulmonary embolism
▪Hyperthyroidism
▪Drug effects (e.g., stimulants)
– In these situations, the body is trying to compensate for reduced 
oxygen delivery.

Mechanism of Sinus Arrhythmia
The sinus node is the pacemaker, but impulses are initiated 
in an irregular pattern. The rate increases as the patient 
breathes in and decreases as the patient breathes out. Each 
impulse is conducted normally through to the ventricles.

• P Wave: Uniform shape; one P wave in front of 
every QRS complex – present, upright, uniform
• PRI: 0.12–0.20 second and constant

Blood Flow in Sinus Arrhythmia
• Normal blood flow pattern is preserved
– Blood still moves through the heart in the usual 
sequence:
– Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs
– Lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body
• There is no abnormal shunting or disruption of 
chamber-to-chamber flow.

pages.title: Clinical Implication of Sinus
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Implication of Sinus 
Arrhythmia
• In healthy individuals, sinus arrhythmia is benign 
and often a sign of good vagal tone.
• It is common in children, young adults, and during 
sleep.
• In older adults, reduced sinus arrhythmia can 
indicate decreased autonomic flexibility.
– It’s essentially a sign that the body is less adaptable to 
stress, activity, and internal changes.

pages.title: Sinus Pause
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Sinus Pause
• Definition: A brief delay in the SA node's firing, typically lasting less 
than 3 seconds. 
• ECG Finding: The next P wave appears on time or with a slight 
delay, but the overall rhythm is preserved. 
• Clinical Significance: Often benign, especially in young or athletic 
individuals. May go unnoticed. 
• Cause: Can be due to increased vagal tone, medications (e.g., beta 
blockers), or intrinsic SA node dysfunction.

pages.title: Sinus Arrest
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Sinus Arrest
• Definition: A longer and more irregular pause in SA node activity, 
usually greater than 3 seconds.
• ECG Finding: The next P wave is late or absent, and the pause is 
not a multiple of the normal P–P interval.
• Clinical Significance: More serious; may lead to syncope, escape 
rhythms, or even asystole if no backup pacemaker takes over.
• Cause: Often due to sick sinus syndrome, ischemia, fibrosis, or drug 
effects.

pages.title: Wandering Pacemaker
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Wandering Pacemaker
The pacemaker site wanders between the sinus node, the atria, 
and the AV junction. Although each impulse originates from a 
different focus, the rate usually remains within a normal range, but 
it can be slower or faster. Conduction through to the ventricles is 
normal.

pages.title: Blood Flow in Wandering Atrial Pacemaker
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Wandering Atrial Pacemaker
Atrial contraction 
remains effective:
Despite the shifting pacemaker sites, 
the atria still contract in a coordinated 
fashion.
The “atrial kick”—which contributes 
~20–30% of ventricular filling—is 
preserved.
Ventricular filling is 
normal:
Since the impulses still reach the AV 
node and ventricles in a timely manner, 
ventricular contraction and cardiac 
output remain largely unaffected.

Mechanism of Premature Atrial Complex
The pacemaker is an irritable focus within the atrium that fires 
prematurely and produces a single ectopic beat. Conduction 
through to the ventricles is normal. This is a single beat, not an 
entire rhythm; the underlying rhythm also must be identified.

pages.title: Blood Flow in Ectopic Complexes
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Ectopic Complexes
• Blood flow may be affected depending on the timing and location of the 
ectopic impulse. 
– Heart may not have sufficient time to fill with blood, resulting in a 
weaker contraction and a reduced stroke volume. 
– Momentary decrease cardiac output, but in healthy individuals, 
isolated ectopic beats rarely cause significant symptoms or 
compromise blood flow.
• Frequent or consecutive ectopic beats, however, may disrupt the 
normal rhythm and coordination of the heart.
– Potentially leading to palpitations, a sensation of skipped beats, or, 
in rare cases, more pronounced circulatory effects if underlying 
cardiac dysfunction is present.

Blood Flow in Atrial Tachycardia
• Blood flow is influenced by the rapid, regular firing of the 
atria, usually at rates between 150 and 250 beats per 
minute. 
• Because the atria contract faster than normal, there is less 
time for them to fill and effectively push blood into the 
ventricles. 
• This can reduce the atrial kick, leading to decreased 
ventricular preload and potentially lowering cardiac output, 
especially if the ventricular response is also rapid.

can be lost in T wave

pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Mechanism of Atrial Flutter
A single irritable focus within the atria issues an impulse that is 
conducted in a rapid, repetitive fashion. To protect the ventricles 
from receiving too many impulses, the AV node blocks some of 
the impulses from being conducted through to the ventricles. 
Those that do get through are conducted normally.

pages.title: Blood Flow in Atrial Flutter
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Atrial Flutter
• Atrial contraction is rapid but coordinated:
– The atria contract too quickly to effectively contribute to ventricular filling.
– The atrial kick—which normally boosts ventricular preload—is diminished 
or lost.
• AV node filters impulses:
– The AV node blocks many of the rapid atrial impulses, often resulting in a 
fixed conduction ratio (e.g., 2:1, 3:1).  MAY BE VARIABLE
– This means the ventricular rate is slower than the atrial rate (e.g., atria at 
300 bpm, ventricles at 150 bpm in 2:1 block).
• Ventricular filling is compromised:
– Shortened diastolic time reduces ventricular filling.
– Cardiac output may drop, especially if the ventricular rate is too fast.

pages.title: Blood Flow in Atrial Flutter
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Atrial Flutter
• Blood stasis risk:
– Although atrial flutter is more organized than AFib, the 
rapid atrial rate still leads to incomplete emptying of 
the atria.
– This can cause blood pooling, especially in the left 
atrial appendage, increasing the risk of thrombus 
formation and stroke.

• Regularity: Atrial rhythm is regular; ventricular 
rhythm is usually regular but can be irregular if 
there is variable block
• Rate: Atrial rate 250–350 bpm; ventricular rate 
varies
• P Wave: Characteristic sawtooth pattern
• PRI: Unable to determine
• QRS: Less than 0.12 second

Mechanism of Atrial Fibrillation
The atria are so irritable that a multitude of foci initiate impulses, 
causing the atria to depolarize repeatedly in a fibrillatory manner. 
The AV node blocks most of the impulses, allowing only a limited 
number through to the ventricles.

pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Atrial Fibrillation
• Atrial contraction is ineffective:
– Normally, atrial systole contributes ~20–30% of 
ventricular filling (the “atrial kick”).
– In AFib, this contribution is lost, reducing preload and 
stroke volume.
• Ventricular response is irregular:
– The AV node filters the chaotic atrial impulses, but the 
ventricular rhythm becomes irregularly irregular.
– This leads to inconsistent diastolic filling times, 
causing variable cardiac output.

pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Atrial Fibrillation
• Blood stasis in the atria:
– Especially in the left atrial appendage, where blood 
can pool due to poor contraction.
– This increases the risk of thrombus formation and 
embolic stroke.

• Rate: Atrial rate greater than 350 bpm; ventricular 
rate varies greatly
• P Wave: No discernible P waves; atrial activity is 
referred to as fibrillatory waves (f waves)
• PRI: Unable to measure
• QRS: Less than 0.12 second

Conduction in Junctional Rhythms
• Escape Mechanism: 
– Inherent pacemaker fails or significantly slows down
– Secondary pacemaker assumes control
• Excitability or Irritability:
– Lower pacemaker significantly speeds up
– Overrides higher pacemaker
• Pacemaker with HIGHEST rate is always the 
controlling pacemaker

pages.title: Blood Flow in Junctional Rhythms
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Junctional Rhythms
• The electrical impulse originates near/in the AV junction rather than the 
sinoatrial node. 
– Atrial contraction may occur out of sync or be absent, which can 
reduce the efficiency of ventricular filling. 
– Leads to a decrease in preload, and consequently, cardiac output 
may be compromised. 
• Blood flow through the heart is therefore less effective, often resulting 
in symptoms such as lightheadedness and fatigue due to diminished 
perfusion to vital organs

pages.title: Conduction in Junctional Rhythms
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Conduction in Junctional Rhythms
• P wave reflects retrograde atrial activation, since 
the impulse originates in the AV junction rather 
than the SA node. 
– P waves may appear inverted in leads II, III, and aVF, 
may be absent, or may occur after the QRS complex 
depending on the timing of atrial and ventricular 
depolarization. In aVR the P waves are UPRIGHT
• The atypical origin and sequence of atrial 
activation contribute to the altered appearance 
and placement of the P wave on the ECG.

Mechanism of Premature Junctional 
Complex
The pacemaker is an irritable focus within the AV junction that fires 
prematurely and produces a single ectopic beat. The atria are 
depolarized via retrograde conduction. Conduction through the 
ventricles is normal. This is a single beat, not an entire rhythm; the 
underlying rhythm also must be identified.

Rules for Premature Junctional
Complex 
• Regularity: Depends on regularity of underlying 
arrhythmia
• Rate: Depends on rate of underlying arrhythmia
• P Wave: Will be inverted; can fall before, during, 
or after the QRS complex
• PRI: Can be measured only if the P wave 
precedes the QRS complex; if measurable, will be 
less than 0.12 second
• QRS: Less than 0.12 second

Mechanism of Junctional Escape 
Rhythm
When higher pacemaker sites fail, the AV junction is left with 
pacemaking responsibility. The atria are depolarized via 
retrograde conduction. Conduction through the ventricles is 
normal.

Supraventricular Tachycardia
• Originates ABOVE the ventricles, typically in the 
SA, atria or the atrioventricular (AV) node.
• SVT can result in palpitations, dizziness, shortness 
of breath, or chest discomfort, and may be 
characterized by a sudden onset and termination. 
(Paroxysmal) SVT
• Causes include:
– Lifestyle  (Stress, Caffeine, Intense Physical Exercise)
– Medical Conditions (Structural, Congenital)
– Electrical Disturbances (Congenital, Medications)

Supraventricular Tachycardia
• Regular, narrow complex tachycardia, with QRS 
duration typically less than 0.12 sec.
• P waves may be absent, buried in the preceding T 
wave, or difficult to distinguish due to the rapid 
rate.
• The ventricular rate is generally between 150 and 
250 beats per minute.

pages.title: Mechanism of First Degree
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Mechanism of First Degree
Heart Block
AV node holds each impulse longer than normal 
before conducting it to the ventricles. Each 
impulse is eventually conducted.

pages.title: Blood Flow in Rhythm with First Degree
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Rhythm with First Degree 
Block
• In first-degree heart block, blood flow remains normal 
because the electrical signal is only delayed—not 
blocked—between the atria and ventricles.
• Mildest form of heart block. It involves a delay in the 
conduction of electrical impulses from the atria to the 
ventricles, typically seen as a prolonged PR interval on an 
electrocardiogram (ECG)—greater than 0.20 seconds

pages.title: Conduction in Rhythm with First Degree
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Conduction in Rhythm with First Degree 
Block
• Electrical delay only: The impulse from the atria to the 
ventricles is slowed, but every impulse still gets through. This 
means the heart continues to beat in a coordinated fashion.
• No interruption in contraction: Because the ventricles still 
contract after each atrial contraction, the heart’s pumping 
action remains effective.
• Normal cardiac output: Blood flow to the body is not 
compromised in isolated first-degree block. The heart’s 
ability to pump blood efficiently is preserved

pages.title: Rules for First Degree Heart Block
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Rules for First Degree Heart Block 
• Regularity: Depends on underlying rhythm
• Rate: Depends on underlying rhythm
• P Wave: Upright and uniform; each P wave will be 
followed by a QRS complex
• PRI: Greater than .20 seconds; constant across 
strip
• QRS: Less than .12 seconds
MUST identify UNDERLYING rhythm

pages.title: Clinical Significance

Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Significance
•Usually asymptomatic: Most people with first-degree AV 
block don’t experience symptoms and may not even know they 
have it.
•Benign condition: It’s often considered a normal variant, 
especially in athletes or individuals with high vagal tone.
•No treatment needed: Unless associated with other cardiac 
conditions or symptoms, first-degree block typically doesn’t 
require intervention

pages.title: Clinical Significance
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Significance
• While first-degree block itself doesn’t affect blood flow, it 
can be a marker of underlying issues:
•Electrolyte imbalances
•Medication effects (e.g., beta-blockers, calcium 
channel blockers)
•Structural heart disease or myocardial infarction
• If symptoms like fatigue, dizziness, or palpitations occur, 
further evaluation may be warranted to rule out 
progression to more serious blocks.

pages.title: Mechanism of Wenckebach (Type I
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Mechanism of Wenckebach (Type I 
Second-Degree Heart Block)
As the sinus node initiates impulses, each one is delayed in 
the AV node a little longer than the preceding one, until one 
impulse is eventually blocked completely. Those impulses 
that are conducted travel normally through the ventricles.

pages.title: Blood Flow in Second Degree, Type I
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Second Degree, Type I 
Block
•Intermittent ventricular contraction: Because some impulses are 
blocked, the ventricles occasionally skip a beat, leading to a brief pause in 
blood ejection.
•Reduced cardiac output: Each missed ventricular contraction means a 
missed opportunity to pump blood to the body, slightly lowering overall 
cardiac output.
•Usually mild: In most cases, especially when the block occurs at rest or 
during sleep, the impact on blood flow is minimal and not clinically 
significant.
•Bradycardia risk: If the dropped beats are frequent, the heart rate may 
slow (bradycardia), which can reduce perfusion to vital organs and cause 
symptoms like dizziness or fatigue

pages.title: Conduction in Second Degree, Type I
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Conduction in Second Degree, Type I 
Block
• Progressive prolongation of PRI until complex is 
dropped and new cycle starts
• “Going, Going Gone”
• Sometimes blocked P will embed in T wave
• Look at PRI
• Look at regularity
• Look at R - R

pages.title: Rules for Wenckebach
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Rules for Wenckebach
• Regularity: Irregular; R-R interval changes 
as PR interval gets longer; characteristic grouped 
beating
• Rate: Usually slightly slower than normal
• P Wave: Upright and uniform; some P waves not 
followed by QRS complexes
• PRI: Progressively lengthens until one P wave is 
not conducted
• QRS: Less than .12 seconds

Clinical Significance
•Often asymptomatic: Many people with Mobitz I block don’t notice any 
symptoms.
•Possible symptoms: If bradycardia becomes pronounced, symptoms 
may include:
•Lightheadedness
•Fatigue
•Shortness of breath
•Monitoring advised: Especially if the block is associated with 
medications (e.g., beta-blockers) or underlying heart disease.

pages.title: Clinical Significance

Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Clinical Significance
•Type I is usually benign, especially in young, healthy 
individuals or athletes.
•Increased concern arises if:
•The block occurs with symptoms
•There’s progression to more severe blocks
•It’s associated with structural heart disease

pages.title: Mechanism of Type II Second Degree
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Mechanism of Type II Second Degree 
Heart Block
The AV node selectively conducts some beats while 
blocking others. Those that are not blocked are conducted 
through to the ventricles, although they may encounter a 
slight delay in the node. Once in the ventricles, conduction 
proceeds normally.

pages.title: Blood Flow in Second Degree, Type II
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow in Second Degree, Type II 
Block
•Intermittent ventricular pauses: Each missed QRS complex 
means the ventricles don’t pump blood during that cycle.
•Reduced cardiac output: Frequent dropped beats can lead to 
bradycardia and insufficient blood flow to the brain and body.
•Risk of syncope: Sudden drops in heart rate and blood 
pressure may cause fainting or dizziness.
•Progression risk: Mobitz II can rapidly progress to complete 
heart block or ventricular asystole, which are life-threatening

pages.title: Conduction in Second Degree, Type II
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Conduction in Second Degree, Type II 
Block
•Sudden conduction failure: Unlike Mobitz I, the PR 
interval remains constant, but some P waves are not 
followed by QRS complexes—meaning the ventricles 
don’t contract.
•No warning: The dropped beats occur without 
progressive delay, making them unpredictable.
•Block location: Typically occurs at/below the AV node 
in the His-Purkinje system, which is more prone to 
structural damage

pages.title: Rules for Type II Second Degree
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Rules for Type II Second Degree
Heart Block 
• Regularity: If the conduction ratio is consistent, the 
R–R interval will be constant, and the rhythm will 
be regular. If the conduction ratio varies, the R–R 
will be irregular.
• Rate: The atrial rate is usually normal (60–100 
bpm). Since many of the atrial impulses are 
blocked, the ventricular rate will usually be in the 
bradycardia range (< 60 bpm), often one-half, 
one-third, or one-fourth of the atrial rate.

pages.title: Rules for Type II Second Degree
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Rules for Type II Second Degree
Heart Block (continued)
• P Waves: P waves are upright and uniform. There 
are always more P waves than QRS complexes.
• PRI: The PRI on conducted beats will be constant 
across the strip, although it might be longer than a 
normal PRI measurement.
• QRS: The QRS complex measurement will be less 
than 0.12 second.

pages.title: Mechanism of Complete Heart
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Mechanism of Complete Heart
Block (CHB)
The block at the AV node is complete. The sinus beats cannot 
penetrate the node and thus are not conducted through to the 
ventricles. An escape mechanism from either the junction or the 
ventricles will take over to pace the ventricles. The atria and 
ventricles function in a totally dissociated fashion.

pages.title: Blood Flow with Third Degree Block
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow with Third Degree Block
• Severely compromised because the atria and 
ventricles beat independently, leading to slow and 
inefficient heart pumping.
• Loss of synchronization of atria and ventricles

pages.title: Blood Flow with Third Degree Block
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Blood Flow with Third Degree Block
•Severely reduced cardiac output: The slow ventricular rate means less blood 
is pumped with each minute, which can lead to inadequate perfusion of vital 
organs.
•Risk of syncope and sudden death: If the escape rhythm fails or is too slow, 
blood flow may drop critically, causing fainting (Stokes-Adams attacks) or even 
cardiac arrest.
•Symptoms: Patients often experience:
•Fatigue
•Dizziness
•Shortness of breath
•Chest pain
•Fainting spells

pages.title: Conduction in Third Degree Block
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Conduction in Third Degree Block
•Electrical dissociation: The atria and ventricles no longer 
communicate electrically. Atrial impulses do not reach the 
ventricles at all.
•Escape rhythm: The ventricles rely on a slower, backup 
pacemaker (junctional or ventricular escape rhythm), often 
producing a heart rate of 30–40 beats per minute.
•AV dissociation: The atria may beat normally (~60–100 
bpm), but the ventricles beat independently and much slower

pages.title: Rules for Complete Heart Block
pages.text:
Copyright © 2017, 2011, 2006 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Rules for Complete Heart Block
• Regularity: Regular
• Rate: AR—usually normal (60–100 bpm)
         VR—40–60 if focus is junctional; 20–40 if 
         focus is ventricular
• P Waves: Upright and uniform; more P waves than QRS 
complexes
• PRI: No relationship between P waves and QRS 
complexes; P waves can occasionally be found 
superimposed on the QRS complex
• QRS: Less than 0.12 second if focus is junctional; 0.12 
second or greater if focus is ventricular

pages.title: Pacemakers
pages.text:
Pacemakers
▪An artificial pacemaker is a device; which, provides an electronic 
signal to make the heart contract when the body’s intrinsic 
pacemakers (such as the SA node) fail. 
▪The goal of an artificial pacemaker is to provide an appropriate 
atrial and/or ventricular rate of contraction; which, will maintain  
adequate end-organ perfusion and sufficient blood pressure.
▪The pacemaker will produce a “spike” or an unnaturally STRAIGHT 
vertical line on the ECG.

pages.title: Pacemakers
pages.text:
Pacemakers
▪Modern pacemakers are programmed with a variety of settings that 
can be tailored to each patient's specific cardiac needs. 
▪Settings control parameters such as the pacing rate, sensitivity to 
the heart's own electrical activity, and the output voltage of the 
impulses delivered. 
▪Physicians adjust these settings:
▪Ensure optimal heart function
▪Minimize unnecessary pacing
▪Extend battery life. 
▪Device can be reprogrammed non-invasively during follow-up 
visits using a specialized programmer that communicates 
wirelessly with the pacemaker.

pages.text:
Pacemakers - Types
▪Transcutaneous
▪External device used in emergency situations
▪Delivers electrical impulses to the heart through

▪Noninvasive approach provides temporary pacing 
support in cases of severe bradycardia or heart 
block until a more permanent solution is 
established
▪Effective in acute settings
▪Uncomfortable due to muscle contractions, not 
suitable for long-term use
Pads placed anteriolateral
May also be placed anterior and posterior
Rate and milliamps are set on monitor to
“capture” rhythm
Rate 60-80, mA 80-100 and 5-10 above threshold

pages.title: Pacemakers
pages.text:
Pacemakers
▪Pulse Generator Settings
▪Demand
▪AKA “on demand” or “synchronous”
▪Monitors the heart’s natural electrical activity
▪Delivers impulses when the heart rate drops below a programmed threshold or when it detects 
missed beats
▪Conserves battery life and minimizes unnecessary pacing
▪Continuous
▪AKA “asynchronous”
▪Delivers electrical impulses at a constant, preset rate regardless of the heart’s own activity
▪Necessary in cases where the heart’s native rhythm is unreliable or absent

pages.title: Pacemakers
pages.text:
Pacemakers
▪Pulse Generator Settings
▪In addition to pacing rate, sensitivity, and output voltage, pulse generators offer several other 
programmable settings to optimize therapy for individual patients
▪Advanced settings enable clinicians to fine-tune the device for each patient’s unique cardiac 
condition and lifestyle needs
▪Triggered Mode
▪Pacemaker delivers an electrical impulse immediately after detecting a specific cardiac 
event, such as a missed or abnormal beat, essentially being "triggered" by the heart's activity
▪Inhibited Mode
▪Pacemaker continuously monitors the heart's natural rhythm and only delivers an electrical 
impulse if it does not detect a heartbeat within a predetermined time frame
▪“Inhibited" from firing when the heart is beating adequately on its own

pages.title: Pacemakers
pages.text:
Pacemakers
▪Reprogramming process is performed 
noninvasively, meaning no surgical procedures or 
incisions are needed
▪Specialized programmer is placed over the skin 
above the pacemaker site, using wireless 
communication to adjust the device's settings 
safely and comfortably
▪Allows physicians to fine-tune the pacemaker's 
operation without exposing the patient to additional 
risks or discomfort

pages.title: Pacemakers
pages.text:
Pacemakers

monitor and regulate heart 
rhythm effectively 
▪Passed through venous system to 
appropriate area(s) for pacing
▪Specially insulated to prevent 
electrical leakage and protect 
surrounding tissue
▪Electrode anchors to heart tissue
▪Ensures reliable signal delivery and 
sensing of the heart’s intrinsic 
electrical activity

pages.title: Pacemakers – Single Chamber Atrial
pages.text:
Pacemakers – Single Chamber Atrial
▪An atrial pacemaker is an electronic device that delivers 
electrical impulses to the atria to regulate heart rate and 
rhythm. 
▪Atrial pacemakers target only the atria. 
▪This device is typically implanted under the skin near the 
collarbone, with a lead (wire) positioned in the right 
atrium.

pages.title: Pacemakers – Single Chamber Atrial
pages.text:
Pacemakers – Single Chamber Atrial
▪Indications for Use
▪Sick sinus syndrome (SSS): When the heart's natural pacemaker is too 
slow or irregular.
▪Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response: To maintain adequate 
heart rate.
▪Atrial standstill: When the atria fail to contract, requiring artificial 
pacing.
▪Other atrial arrhythmias: When medication or other treatments are 
ineffective.

pages.title: Pacemakers – Single Chamber Atrial
pages.text:
Pacemakers – Single Chamber Atrial
▪The pacemaker continuously monitors the heart's electrical 
activity. 
▪If it detects a pause or a rate that falls below a programmed 
threshold, it sends a small electrical signal to the atrium to prompt 
a contraction. 
▪This helps maintain a normal heart rhythm and prevents 
symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, or fainting.

Pacemakers – Single Chamber Ventricular
▪Ventricular pacemakers are devices designed to regulate the heartbeat by 
delivering electrical impulses directly to the ventricles, the heart’s main 
pumping chambers. 
▪These pacemakers are commonly used in patients with conditions such as 
complete heart block or ventricular arrhythmias, where the heart’s natural 
electrical system fails to maintain an adequate rate or rhythm.
▪Benefits: By ensuring the ventricles contract regularly and efficiently, 
ventricular pacemakers help prevent symptoms like fatigue, dizziness, and 
fainting.

Pacemakers – Dual Chamber
▪Dual chamber pacemakers are advanced devices that coordinate electrical 
stimulation to both the atria and ventricles
▪Closely mimics the heart’s natural rhythm. 
▪They are particularly beneficial for patients with conditions that impair 
communication between the upper and lower chambers, such as atrioventricular 
block or certain types of bradycardia. 
▪By synchronizing the contraction of both chambers:
▪Help optimize cardiac output 
▪Reduce symptoms like fatigue, dizziness, and palpitations.

pages.title: Pacemakers – Biventricular
pages.text:
Pacemakers – Biventricular
▪Biventricular pacemakers, also known as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) 
devices, are specialized pacemakers designed to improve the coordination of 
contractions between the left and right ventricles. 
▪These devices are most often used in patients with heart failure who have evidence of 
ventricular dyssynchrony, where the ventricles do not beat together efficiently. 
▪By synchronizing the timing of ventricular contractions, biventricular pacemakers can 
significantly enhance cardiac output and reduce symptoms associated with heart 
failure.
▪NOTE:  Should appear as a single Ventricular spike but if slightly out of sync it may 
appear as two spikes

pages.title: Stable Angina
pages.text:
Stable Angina
▪What is Stable Angina?
▪Stable angina is a type of chest pain or discomfort caused by reduced blood flow 
to the heart muscle. 
▪Typically occurs during physical exertion or emotional stress and is relieved by 
rest or medication (e.g., nitroglycerin). 
▪Most common form of angina and is usually a symptom of coronary artery 
disease (CAD), where plaque buildup narrows the arteries supplying blood to the 
heart.

pages.title: Stable Angina
pages.text:
Stable Angina
▪Symptoms

Chest pain or discomfort described as pressure, heaviness, squeezing, 
burning, or indigestion-like

Pain may radiate to left shoulder, arm, neck, jaw

Shortness of breath

Nausea, dizziness, fatigue
▪Episodes are predictable, last about 5 minutes or less, and occur during 
exertion or stress.

pages.title: Unstable Angina - NSTEMI
pages.text:
Unstable Angina - NSTEMI
▪Unstable angina is a medical emergency and a type of acute coronary syndrome 
(ACS). It occurs when the heart muscle does not receive enough oxygen due to 
sudden reduction in blood flow, usually caused by:

Plaque rupture in a coronary artery

Blood clot formation (thrombosis)

Occasionally, coronary artery spasm [

Unlike stable angina, which is predictable and relieved by rest or medication, 
unstable angina:

Happens unexpectedly, often at rest

Is more severe and prolonged

Not relieved by nitroglycerin or rest
▪Indicates high risk of heart attack or sudden death

pages.text:
Unstable Angina - NSTEMI



blocked, reducing blood flow and oxygen supply to the heart muscle. Unlike 
STEMI, it does not show ST-segment elevation on an ECG, but it still causes 
myocardial damage and is considered a medical emergency. 
▪Causes

Atherosclerotic plaque rupture 
 partial blockage by clot

pages.title: Bundle Branch Blocks – Some Causes
pages.text:
Bundle Branch Blocks – Some Causes
Right bundle branch block
• Blood clot in the lungs (pulmonary 
embolism)
• Heart attack (myocardial infarction)
• Heart structure problems that are 
present at birth (congenital heart 
defects) — such as a hole in the wall 
separating the upper chambers of the 
heart (atrial septal defect)
• High blood pressure in the pulmonary 
arteries (pulmonary hypertension)
• Inflammation of the heart muscle 
(myocarditis)
Left bundle branch block
• Heart attack (myocardial 
infarction)
• High blood pressure 
(hypertension)
• Inflammation of the heart 
muscle (myocarditis)
• Thickened, stiffened or 
weakened heart muscle 
(cardiomyopathy)

pages.title: Right Bundle Branch Blocks
pages.text:
Right Bundle Branch Blocks
•QRS duration > 120ms
•RSR’ pattern in V1-3 
(“M-shaped” QRS 
complex)
•Wide, slurred S wave in 
lateral leads (I, aVL, V5-
6)

pages.title: Left Bundle Branch Blocks
pages.text:
Left Bundle Branch Blocks
•Dominant S wave in V1, if 
R wave it may be very 
small
•Broad monophasic R 
wave in lateral leads (I, 
aVL, V5-6)
•Absence of Q and S waves 
in lateral leads
•Often notched

pages.title: Special Situations

Special Situations
▪Diagnosis is confirmed by the 
presence of ST elevation in the 
right-sided leads (V3R-V6R)
▪V1 is the only standard ECG lead 
that looks directly at the right 
ventricle
▪Lead III is more rightward facing 
than lead II and hence more 
sensitive to the injury current 
produced by the right ventricle

SUMMARY
pages.text:
SUMMARY
▪Looped circuit circulation is vital to the needs of the body.
▪Pulmonary circuit MUST remove carbon dioxide and deliver 
oxygen rich blood TO the heart. (RIGHT SIDE of Heart)
▪Systemic circuit MUST supply oxygen rich blood to meet the 
demands of the cells of the body. (LEFT SIDE of Heart)
▪Cardiac circulation pathway is part of systemic circuit
▪Must be functioning optimally to meet the high demands of 
the heart tissue for OXYGEN.
